name: Fiordland National Park
description: Fiordland is New Zealand's largest national park at 12,607 km², encompassing spectacular fjords including Milford Sound carved by glacial action over millions of years. Part of the Te Wāhipounamu UNESCO World Heritage Site, it shelters rare species including the takahē, Fiordland crested penguin and bottlenose dolphins. Milford Sound receives over 7 metres of rainfall annually, feeding hundreds of waterfalls that cascade directly into the sea in one of the world's most dramatically beautiful natural settings.
history: The Māori navigated and settled Fiordland for centuries, valuing it for pounamu greenstone collected along its rivers. The national park was established in 1952. UNESCO listed Te Wāhipounamu in 1990, encompassing Fiordland along with three adjacent parks. The Milford Track, opened in 1888, was described as 'the finest walk in the world' by a London newspaper in 1908 — a description that has brought generations of international trampers to this remote and magnificent landscape.

name: Plitvice Lakes National Park
description: Plitvice Lakes National Park contains a chain of 16 terraced emerald lakes interconnected by waterfalls, flowing through a limestone canyon. The lakes' vivid turquoise and green colours result from minerals, organisms and light interacting with the water chemistry. Spanning 295 km², Croatia's oldest and largest national park shelters brown bears, wolves, lynx and over 120 bird species in its mixed beech and fir forests around the famous lake system that changes colour with the seasons and weather.
history: Established in 1949, Plitvice was among Yugoslavia's first protected areas. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 1979. During the Croatian War of Independence (1991–1995) the park was occupied by Serbian forces and its rangers were among the first casualties of the war; the park today commemorates this period as part of its heritage. Post-war restoration and booming tourism have made it Croatia's single most visited tourist attraction.

name: Göbekli Tepe
description: Göbekli Tepe is the world's oldest known monumental structure, built approximately 11,500 years ago — 7,000 years before Stonehenge. Its T-shaped limestone pillars weighing up to 20 tonnes are carved with animal reliefs and arranged in circular enclosures. Deliberately buried around 8,000 BC and preserved beneath a hill, its existence overturned the assumption that monumental architecture required settled agriculture — it was built by hunter-gatherers in one of humanity's most remarkable early collective achievements.
history: First examined in 1963 by archaeologists who dismissed it as a medieval cemetery. Klaus Schmidt began systematic excavation in 1994 and recognised its extraordinary prehistoric significance, working the site until his death in 2014. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 2018. Less than 5% of the site has been excavated — ground-penetrating radar surveys suggest up to 20 additional stone circles buried beneath the plateau, potentially making future discoveries even more transformative than what has already been revealed.

name: Palace of Versailles
description: The Palace of Versailles and its 800-hectare gardens represent the apotheosis of French absolute monarchy and the most influential palace complex in European history. Louis XIV's creation set the template for royal grandeur imitated across Europe. The Hall of Mirrors — 73 metres of arched windows facing 357 mirrors — became the most famous room in Europe. The formal gardens by André Le Nôtre, with their fountains, canals and sculpture, remain the definitive statement of French formal landscape design and the ideal of order imposed on nature.
history: Construction began in 1661 under Louis XIV who made Versailles the seat of French government. The palace was the royal residence until Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette were forced to return to Paris by a revolutionary mob in October 1789. UNESCO inscribed Versailles as a World Heritage Site in 1979. The German Empire was proclaimed here in 1871, and the Treaty of Versailles ending World War I was signed in the Hall of Mirrors in 1919 — the same room, 48 years apart, bookending a century of European catastrophe.

name: Alhambra, Granada
description: The Alhambra in Granada is the finest surviving example of Moorish architecture in the world — a palace and fortress built by the Nasrid sultans between the 13th and 15th centuries. Its Court of the Lions with slender alabaster columns, geometric tile and plasterwork of the Comares Palace, and Generalife gardens represent an aesthetic experience of extraordinary refinement. The palace's arabesque decoration, muqarnas vaulting and water garden integration represent the apex of Andalusian Islamic art.
history: The Alhambra was the seat of the last Muslim sultanate in Western Europe until the Reconquista expelled the Moors from Granada in January 1492 — the same year Columbus sailed for the Americas, tying together two world-defining events. Washington Irving lived in the Alhambra in 1829 and wrote Tales of the Alhambra, sparking the romantic revival of interest in Moorish Spain across Europe and America. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 1984.

name: Dubrovnik Old City
description: Dubrovnik's Old City is the best-preserved medieval walled city in the Mediterranean — limestone walls, Baroque churches, marble-paved streets and terracotta-roofed palaces enclosed within 2 km of intact medieval fortifications. The Republic of Ragusa, ruling the city from 1358 to 1808, was a remarkable mercantile republic that maintained independence between the Ottoman and Venetian empires through skilled diplomacy. George Bernard Shaw called Dubrovnik 'the pearl of the Adriatic' and that reputation has only grown.
history: Founded in the 7th century and developed as the independent Republic of Ragusa, which abolished slavery in 1416 and had one of Europe's first quarantine systems — remarkable innovations for a medieval city-state. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 1979. During the 1991–1992 siege by Yugoslav Army forces, 68% of the Old City buildings were damaged. Restoration over the following decade is considered a model of post-war cultural heritage recovery globally.

name: Machu Picchu
description: The 15th-century Inca citadel of Machu Picchu perches at 2,430 m above sea level in the Andes of Peru — one of the world's most dramatic archaeological sites. Built around 1450 at the height of the Inca Empire and abandoned a century later, its precise stonework, agricultural terraces and astronomical alignments reflect extraordinary engineering sophistication. UNESCO listed it in 1983 and it was declared a New Wonder of the World in 2007. Approximately 1 million visitors annually raise ongoing conservation concerns about the fragile site.
history: 'Discovered' by American historian Hiram Bingham III in 1911, guided to the site by local farmer Melchor Arteaga — though indigenous Quechua communities had always known of its existence. Bingham removed thousands of artefacts to Yale University, which returned them to Peru in 2012 after decades of diplomatic pressure. Current conservation concerns focus on the approximately 1 million annual visitors whose presence damages the fragile Inca stonework and surrounding cloud forest ecosystem, threatening the integrity of this irreplaceable heritage site.

name: Stonehenge
description: Stonehenge on Salisbury Plain is the world's most famous prehistoric monument — a ring of standing stones erected in multiple phases between 3000 and 1500 BC. The largest sarsen stones weigh up to 25 tonnes and were transported 25 km from Marlborough Downs. The bluestones originated in the Preseli Hills of Wales, 250 km distant. The monument is aligned with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset, indicating sophisticated astronomical knowledge. Despite 200 years of investigation, its precise purpose remains actively debated by archaeologists and scientists worldwide.
history: Constructed in multiple phases over 1,500 years. Used as a burial ground for at least 500 years. UNESCO inscribed Stonehenge as part of the Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites World Heritage Site in 1986. Modern Druid ceremonies were banned from 1985 to 2000 following conflicts with police; access is now permitted for solstice celebrations. A new visitor centre opened in 2013, and ongoing excavations continue to reveal new details about the monument's builders, purpose and the vast sacred landscape that surrounds it.

name: Great Pyramids of Giza
description: The Great Pyramids of Giza are the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the only ones still standing. The Great Pyramid of Khufu, completed around 2560 BC, stood as the world's tallest man-made structure for 3,800 years. The three pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, along with the Great Sphinx, represent the apex of ancient Egyptian engineering. The precision with which 2.3 million limestone blocks were quarried, transported and laid continues to astonish modern engineers and inspire competing scientific theories about construction methods.
history: Built during the Fourth Dynasty of ancient Egypt's Old Kingdom over approximately 85 years. Recent papyrus discoveries at Wadi al-Jarf document the logistics of pyramid construction including the transport of limestone by boat. UNESCO inscribed Memphis and its Necropolis as a World Heritage Site in 1979. The site faces ongoing threats from urban encroachment as Cairo's suburbs have expanded to the pyramid plateau boundary, creating one of the world's most dramatic juxtapositions of ancient monument and modern sprawling metropolis.

name: Angkor Wat
description: Angkor Wat is the world's largest religious monument at 162.6 hectares, and the best-preserved temple of the Khmer Empire. Built in the early 12th century by King Suryavarman II as a Hindu temple later converted to Buddhism, it features five lotus-shaped towers and 3 km of bas-relief galleries. At its peak, the Angkor complex housed up to one million people — the world's largest pre-industrial city — in a vast hydraulic civilisation that managed water across the Mekong floodplain using extraordinary engineering.
history: The Khmer Empire's capital from approximately the 9th to 15th centuries AD. Abandoned in 1431 following Thai invasions and climate-driven droughts. French naturalist Henri Mouhot 'rediscovered' the site for European audiences in 1860. UNESCO inscribed Angkor as a World Heritage Site in 1992 and coordinated restoration following the Khmer Rouge era devastation. LiDAR surveys since 2012 have revealed a vast hidden urban and hydraulic landscape surrounding the temples, showing the true scale of the Khmer civilisation.

name: Petra
description: Petra is the ancient Nabataean city carved into rose-red sandstone cliffs in southern Jordan. The Treasury (Al-Khazneh) with its 40-metre facade carved directly from the rock face is the iconic centrepiece of a city that controlled ancient spice and silk trade routes. Over 800 individual monuments including temples, tombs and a 6,000-seat theatre, all carved from living rock, were created by the Nabataean people between the 4th century BC and 2nd century AD in this extraordinary and awe-inspiring geological setting.
history: Served as the Nabataean Kingdom capital from around the 4th century BC, growing wealthy by taxing caravans. Declined after Roman annexation in 106 AD and an earthquake in 363 AD. Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt rediscovered it for Europeans in 1812, disguising himself as a Muslim pilgrim. UNESCO inscribed Petra in 1985 and it was named a New Wonder of the World in 2007. Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989) featured its iconic facade, dramatically increasing global awareness of this extraordinary hidden city.

name: Chichen Itza
description: Chichen Itza was one of the greatest cities of Maya civilisation, flourishing between 600 and 1200 AD. The El Castillo pyramid casts a serpent shadow on its staircase at the spring and autumn equinoxes — a calendar in stone with 365 steps. The Sacred Cenote, Great Ball Court (the largest in ancient Mesoamerica), and the Observatory reflect the Maya's extraordinary knowledge of astronomy and mathematics. The site receives over 2 million visitors annually and remains Mexico's second most visited archaeological site after Teotihuacan.
history: Founded around 600 AD and reaching its height between 900–1200 AD. The Sacred Cenote has yielded hundreds of skeletal remains thrown in as ritual sacrifices. Largely abandoned by the time Spanish conquistadors arrived in the 16th century. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 1988 and it was declared a New Wonder of the World in 2007. Restoration works over 60 years have stabilised the pyramids, though the methodology of reconstruction remains a subject of ongoing scientific debate among Mesoamerican archaeologists.

name: Colosseum
description: The Colosseum in Rome is the largest amphitheatre ever built — a 50,000-seat oval arena completed in 80 AD that hosted gladiatorial combat, animal hunts, public executions and theatrical performances for over 400 years. Its elliptical design, vaulted concrete construction and sophisticated crowd management system of 80 entrances made it an engineering masterpiece that has influenced stadium and arena design for two millennia. Two-thirds of the original structure remains standing despite centuries of earthquake damage and stone quarrying for other buildings.
history: Commissioned by Emperor Vespasian around 70 AD and completed by his son Titus in 80 AD, built on the site of Nero's private lake using 100,000 tonnes of travertine limestone. Gladiatorial combat continued until approximately 435 AD. The building was later used as a fortress, church, cemetery and quarry before recognition as a historic monument in the 19th century. Today it is Italy's most visited monument, receiving over 7 million visitors annually, and is one of the world's most recognised symbols of ancient Rome's power and engineering ambition.

name: Mosi-oa-Tunya / Victoria Falls
description: Victoria Falls, known locally as Mosi-oa-Tunya — 'the smoke that thunders' — is one of the largest and most spectacular waterfalls on Earth, on the Zambezi River between Zimbabwe and Zambia. At full flood the curtain of water plunges more than 100 metres into a narrow gorge, sending up a column of mist visible for kilometres. The falls support a lush rainforest sustained entirely by their spray. Activities range from rainforest walks and helicopter flights to white-water rafting in the gorges below.
history: The falls have been known and revered by local peoples for centuries before the Scottish explorer David Livingstone reached them in 1855 and named them for Queen Victoria. They became a focal point of colonial-era tourism and the dramatic Victoria Falls Bridge was completed in 1905. Today they are shared and jointly promoted by Zimbabwe and Zambia. UNESCO inscribed Mosi-oa-Tunya/Victoria Falls in 1989 for its outstanding natural beauty.

name: Palace and Park of Versailles
description: The Palace of Versailles, outside Paris, is the most magnificent royal residence in Europe and a symbol of absolute monarchy. Its lavish state apartments, crowned by the dazzling Hall of Mirrors, set a standard of opulence imitated across the continent. The vast formal gardens, with their geometric parterres, fountains and canals, are as celebrated as the palace itself. Together they represent the height of French art and the ambitions of the Sun King.
history: Louis XIV transformed his father's hunting lodge into a colossal palace and moved the royal court there in 1682, centralising power around himself. Versailles became the political heart of France and the stage for elaborate court ritual until the Revolution. The Treaty of Versailles, ending the First World War, was later signed in the Hall of Mirrors. UNESCO inscribed the palace and park in 1979 as a masterpiece of 17th- and 18th-century French art.

name: Alhambra, Generalife and Albayzín
description: The Alhambra is a breathtaking palace and fortress complex crowning a hill above Granada in southern Spain. Within its red walls lie courtyards, fountains, and halls adorned with intricate stucco, tilework and carved inscriptions of unparalleled refinement. The adjacent Generalife gardens offer cool terraces, pools and views over the city and the snow-capped Sierra Nevada. Below, the whitewashed Albayzín quarter preserves the medieval Moorish street plan.
history: The Alhambra was developed primarily in the 13th and 14th centuries as the residence of the Nasrid rulers, the last Muslim dynasty in Spain. It represents the final flowering of Islamic art and architecture in the Iberian Peninsula. After the Christian conquest of Granada in 1492 it passed to Spanish monarchs, who added Renaissance elements. UNESCO inscribed the Alhambra, Generalife and Albayzín in 1984 as a supreme expression of Moorish civilisation.

name: Old Town of Dubrovnik
description: The old town of Dubrovnik is a perfectly preserved walled city on the Adriatic coast of Croatia, often called the 'Pearl of the Adriatic'. Its massive stone ramparts encircle a compact maze of polished limestone streets, churches, palaces and fountains. Walking the city walls offers spectacular views over the terracotta rooftops and the blue sea beyond. Its dramatic setting has made it a beloved travel destination and film location.
history: Dubrovnik flourished as the maritime Republic of Ragusa, a wealthy and remarkably independent trading state that rivalled Venice from the medieval period. Its diplomacy and commerce allowed it to remain self-governing for centuries. A devastating earthquake in 1667 and shelling during the 1991-92 conflict both damaged the city, which was carefully restored each time. UNESCO inscribed the old town in 1979.

name: The British Museum
description: The British Museum in London is one of the greatest and most visited museums in the world, holding a collection that spans two million years of human history. Its galleries display treasures from every continent, including the Rosetta Stone, the Parthenon sculptures and vast Egyptian, Assyrian and Asian collections. The soaring glass-roofed Great Court at its centre is the largest covered public square in Europe. Admission is free, in keeping with its founding ideal of universal access to knowledge.
history: The museum was established in 1753 around the collection of the physician and naturalist Sir Hans Sloane, becoming the first national public museum in the world. Its holdings expanded enormously during the era of empire and exploration, often by means now subject to debate over ownership. The present grand Neoclassical building was completed in the mid-19th century. It remains a centre of scholarship and a focal point in discussions about cultural restitution.
photo_author: Luke Massey & the Greater London National Park City Initiative

name: Musée du Louvre
description: The Louvre in Paris is the world's most visited museum and home to tens of thousands of works of art across vast galleries on the banks of the Seine. Its collections range from ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian antiquities to European painting and sculpture, crowned by the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo. The glass pyramid in the courtyard, added in 1989, forms a striking modern entrance to the historic palace. A visit can occupy days and still leave much unseen.
history: The Louvre began as a medieval fortress and grew into a magnificent royal palace over the centuries. It opened as a public museum in 1793 during the French Revolution, displaying art seized from the crown and the church. Napoleon expanded its collections through conquest, and the museum has grown continuously ever since. It stands as a symbol of France's cultural heritage and the democratisation of art.

name: Prado Museum
description: The Prado in Madrid is one of the world's finest art museums, renowned above all for its incomparable collection of European painting. Its walls hold the greatest assemblage of works by Velázquez, Goya and El Greco, alongside masterpieces by Titian, Bosch and Rubens. Velázquez's Las Meninas and Goya's haunting 'black paintings' are among its most celebrated treasures. The Neoclassical building anchors Madrid's grand boulevard of museums.
history: The museum opened in 1819, built around the magnificent collections amassed by the Spanish royal family over the centuries. The Habsburg and Bourbon monarchs were avid patrons, which gives the Prado its particular depth in Spanish, Italian and Flemish art. The building, originally designed to house a natural-history collection, was repurposed as a picture gallery. The Prado forms part of Madrid's UNESCO-listed cultural landscape of the Paseo del Prado.

name: State Hermitage Museum
description: The State Hermitage in Saint Petersburg is one of the largest and oldest museums in the world, spread across the opulent Winter Palace and adjoining buildings. Its collection of some three million items spans world art from antiquity to the modern era, including masterpieces by Rembrandt, Leonardo and the Impressionists. The lavish state rooms of the former imperial residence are works of art in themselves. The scale is staggering, with galleries that could take days to explore.
history: The museum was founded in 1764 when Empress Catherine the Great acquired a major collection of European paintings. Successive tsars expanded the holdings, which became the private gallery of the imperial family. After the 1917 revolution the collections were nationalised and the palace opened fully to the public. The Hermitage forms part of the UNESCO-listed historic centre of Saint Petersburg.

name: Angkor
description: Angkor in Cambodia is one of the most important archaeological sites in the world, the vast remains of the capital of the Khmer Empire spread across the jungle. Its crowning glory is Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument ever built, its five towers a symbol of the nation. The enigmatic stone faces of the Bayon and the tree-entwined ruins of Ta Prohm are equally famous. Sunrise over the temples is one of the great travel experiences of Asia.
history: The Khmer Empire ruled much of Southeast Asia from Angkor between the 9th and 15th centuries, building hundreds of temples and an immense network of canals and reservoirs. Angkor Wat was constructed in the early 12th century as a Hindu temple before becoming a Buddhist site. The capital was eventually abandoned and reclaimed by the forest. UNESCO inscribed Angkor in 1992 as a masterpiece of Khmer civilisation.

name: Borobudur Temple Compounds
description: Borobudur on the island of Java is the largest Buddhist temple in the world, a colossal stepped pyramid rising from the surrounding plain. Its terraces are adorned with thousands of relief panels and hundreds of Buddha statues, many seated within perforated bell-shaped stupas. Pilgrims ascend through symbolic levels representing the path to enlightenment, culminating in a great central stupa. At dawn it emerges from the mist with volcanoes silhouetted behind it.
history: Borobudur was built around the 8th and 9th centuries under the Sailendra dynasty as a grand monument to Buddhist cosmology. It was abandoned for centuries, possibly after volcanic eruptions and the decline of Buddhism on Java, and lay buried under ash and vegetation. It was rediscovered in the early 19th century and later extensively restored. UNESCO inscribed Borobudur in 1991 as one of the greatest Buddhist monuments in the world.

name: National Museum, New Delhi
description: The National Museum in New Delhi holds one of the most comprehensive collections of Indian art and history, spanning five thousand years. Its galleries display Indus Valley artefacts, exquisite sculpture, miniature paintings, jewellery and decorative arts from across the subcontinent. Treasures include relics associated with the Buddha and masterpieces of bronze and stone carving. It offers a sweeping introduction to the cultural wealth of India.
history: The museum had its origins in an exhibition of Indian art shown in London in 1947-48, the objects from which formed the nucleus of a new national collection. It opened in its permanent building in New Delhi in 1960. Over the decades its holdings grew to encompass the breadth of Indian civilisation. It serves as the principal repository of the nation's artistic heritage.

name: National Palace Museum
description: The National Palace Museum in Taipei holds one of the world's greatest collections of Chinese art, numbering nearly 700,000 objects. Its treasures span millennia, from ancient bronzes and jades to imperial paintings, calligraphy, ceramics and rare books. Famous pieces such as the jadeite cabbage and the meat-shaped stone draw crowds of admirers. The depth of the imperial collection is unrivalled.
history: The collection originated in the imperial holdings of the Chinese emperors, accumulated over a thousand years. Much of it was evacuated from Beijing as conflict engulfed China in the 20th century and ultimately moved to Taiwan around 1949. The museum opened in Taipei in 1965 to house and display these treasures. It remains a focal point of Chinese cultural heritage and a subject of cross-strait significance.

name: Tikal National Park
description: Tikal in the rainforests of northern Guatemala is one of the most spectacular Maya cities, its towering temple-pyramids rising above the jungle canopy. The steep stone temples, plazas and palaces of the ancient city are alive with the calls of howler monkeys and toucans. Climbing to the top of a temple to look out over the forest and other pyramids is a magical experience. The setting amid pristine rainforest makes it both an archaeological and a natural wonder.
history: Tikal was one of the most powerful city-states of the Maya civilisation, flourishing between roughly 200 and 900 CE. At its peak it may have had a population well over 50,000 and dominated much of the lowland Maya world. The city was abandoned around the 10th century and reclaimed by the forest. UNESCO inscribed Tikal in 1979 as one of the first mixed cultural and natural World Heritage Sites.

name: Rapa Nui National Park (Easter Island)
description: Rapa Nui, or Easter Island, is one of the most remote inhabited places on Earth, famous for its enigmatic stone statues. Nearly 900 monolithic figures called moai, carved with massive heads and torsos, stand or lie across the windswept island. The largest were transported and raised on stone platforms facing inland over the communities they watched over. The mystery of how and why they were created lends the island a haunting power.
history: Polynesian settlers reached the island around the 12th to 13th century CE and developed a remarkable society that carved and erected the moai over several centuries. Environmental degradation and contact with the outside world led to dramatic social collapse and population loss. The island was annexed by Chile in 1888. UNESCO inscribed Rapa Nui National Park in 1995 to protect this extraordinary cultural landscape.

name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
description: The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York is the largest art museum in the Americas and one of the most comprehensive in the world. Its vast galleries span five thousand years of art, from Egyptian temples and Greek sculpture to European masters and modern works. Highlights include the reconstructed Temple of Dendur, arms and armour, and an unrivalled painting collection. A visit can fill many hours and still cover only a fraction of the collection.
history: The museum was founded in 1870 by a group of citizens determined to bring art and art education to the American people. It grew rapidly through gifts and acquisitions into a collection of more than two million objects. Its landmark building on Fifth Avenue beside Central Park has been expanded many times. The Met remains one of the cultural anchors of New York City.

name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
description: The Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History on the National Mall in Washington is one of the most visited museums in the world. Its halls hold the giant African bush elephant in the rotunda, dinosaur skeletons, the Hope Diamond and vast collections from the natural world. Exhibits cover human origins, ocean life, gems and minerals and the diversity of cultures. Admission is free, in keeping with the Smithsonian's public mission.
history: The museum opened in 1910 as part of the Smithsonian Institution, established in 1846 for 'the increase and diffusion of knowledge'. It holds one of the largest natural-history collections on Earth, numbering well over a hundred million specimens. Behind its public galleries lies a major centre of scientific research. It remains one of the cornerstones of the Smithsonian complex.

name: Meteora
description: Meteora in central Greece is a breathtaking landscape of monasteries perched atop towering pillars of rock. Sheer columns of sandstone rise hundreds of metres from the plain, crowned by centuries-old Orthodox monasteries that seem to float in the air. Once accessible only by removable ladders and nets, several monasteries can now be visited by steps cut into the rock. The combination of dramatic geology and remote spirituality is unforgettable.
history: The strange rock pillars formed over millions of years through erosion of an ancient river delta. From the 14th century, Orthodox monks climbed the pinnacles to build hermitages and monasteries, seeking refuge and solitude in the heights. At their peak more than twenty monasteries crowned the rocks; six remain active today. UNESCO inscribed Meteora in 1988 for its unique union of nature and monastic life.

name: Pompeii
description: Pompeii near Naples is the most famous archaeological site in the world, a Roman city frozen in time by a volcanic eruption. Its streets, houses, shops, baths and theatres survive in extraordinary detail, with frescoes, mosaics and even graffiti still in place. Plaster casts of the victims capture their final moments with haunting immediacy. Walking its paved streets offers an unparalleled window into everyday Roman life.
history: Pompeii was a prosperous Roman town until the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE buried it under metres of ash and pumice. The ash sealed and preserved the city almost perfectly until its rediscovery and excavation from the 18th century. The finds revolutionised understanding of Roman daily life and art. UNESCO inscribed Pompeii, with Herculaneum and Torre Annunziata, in 1997.

name: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
description: The Egyptian Museum in Cairo holds the world's most extensive collection of ancient Egyptian antiquities. Its galleries overflow with statues, sarcophagi, mummies and treasures spanning thousands of years of pharaonic civilisation. The dazzling golden funerary mask and treasures of Tutankhamun have long been among its star attractions. The sheer density of priceless artefacts is overwhelming.
history: The museum opened in 1902 in its distinctive salmon-coloured building on Tahrir Square to house Egypt's vast archaeological wealth. For more than a century it served as the principal home of the nation's treasures. Many of its most famous pieces, including the Tutankhamun collection, are being transferred to the new Grand Egyptian Museum near the pyramids. The historic museum remains a landmark of Egyptian heritage.
